props.title: Céline and Julie Go Boating

sections.content: Céline and Julie Go Boating (1974) stands as Jacques Rivette's magnum opus of playful experimentation, weaving a 3-hour labyrinth of reality-bending narrative. The film follows librarian Julie (Dominique Labourier) and magician Céline (Juliet Berto) through a dreamlike Paris, their friendship sparking a mysterious investigation into a haunted house where melodrama eternally repeats. It directly influenced Mulholland Drive (2001) and Persona (1966) in its exploration of feminine doubles and reality-blurring storytelling. The candy-as-memory device later echoes in films like Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind (2004).

sections.content: The film's structure revolutionized narrative cinema by treating plot as a playground rather than a prison. Like Last Year at Marienbad (1961), it creates a puzzle box of repeated scenes and shifting perspectives. But where Resnais aimed for cold modernism, Rivette infuses his experiment with warmth and wit. The haunted house sequences, where Céline and Julie take turns witnessing/participating in a Victorian melodrama, prefigure the reality-bending structures of Inception (2010) and Synecdoche, New York (2008).

The film's influence on female friendship narratives cannot be overstated. Its playful, conspiratorial bond between the leads echoes through Ghost World (2001), Bound (1996), and Mulholland Drive (2001). The way it treats female imagination as a force for reality-reshaping liberation influenced In the Cut (2003) and The Double Life of Véronique (1991). SUBHEAD: The Magic of Memory and Performance

movies.title: La Belle Noiseuse
movies.slug: Rivette's four-hour meditation on art and creation, featuring similar themes of female agency

sections.content: Rivette's use of theatrical performance as reality-warping device influenced generations of filmmakers. The house sequences, where memories are accessed through magical candy, create a meta-commentary on cinema itself. This technique of using performance to access hidden truths appears in Holy Motors (2012), Inland Empire (2006), and The Science of Sleep (2006). The film's length and repetitions create a hypnotic effect that Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles (1975) would later employ to different ends.
